beliefs.practice: Read the MongoDB-style connection string from the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable and never hard-code, log, or commit it; use a .env.example with a placeholder.
Always enable TLS/SSL on the MongoDB client (tls=True / ssl=True) and validate server certificates when connecting to the DocumentDB cluster.
Use a managed secret store (Azure Key Vault) or an environment-only secret mechanism for the connection string and API keys rather than embedding them in code or repository files.
Configure the MongoDB driver connection pool (maxPoolSize, minPoolSize) and timeouts (serverSelectionTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS) explicitly to match app concurrency instead of relying on defaults.
Use Decimal128 (or a fixed-point numeric type) for storing monetary and regulatory values (risk-weighted assets, CET1 amounts) to avoid floating-point rounding errors.

Design documents to embed frequently accessed small subdocuments (e.g., instrument metadata) and reference large or growing collections (e.g., time series) to balance read performance and update costs.

Create indexes supporting the aggregation pipeline: add compound indexes on fields used in $match and $group (e.g., account_id, risk_type, report_date) so the pipeline filters early and scans fewer documents.
When aggregating sums, $match as the first stage, then $project to include only numeric fields required for sum/group to minimize network and memory use; verify with explain() that the index is used.
For financial aggregations, set an explicit readConcern and writeConcern appropriate for correctness (e.g., majority readConcern for critical reads) and be aware of the cost/latency trade-offs.
Implement retries with exponential backoff for transient network and server errors; make aggregation and write operations idempotent or detect duplicate execution to avoid double-counting.
Use server-side aggregation (MongoDB aggregate pipelines) to compute risk-weighted sums rather than fetching all documents and summing client-side to reduce data transfer and RU/IO consumption.

If using vector search, store vectors in a dedicated field and create the provider-specific approximate nearest neighbor index (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) with tuned parameters (e.g., efConstruction, M, ef) appropriate for recall/latency; normalize vectors before indexing/searching.
Limit the dimensionality and cardinality of vector fields and avoid unbounded growth of vector-indexed collections to keep index build and query cost predictable.

Choose a sharding / partition key with high cardinality and that is present in common queries (e.g., account_id or client_id) to avoid hot partitions if the cluster is sharded or provisioned with partitioning.
When seeding sample data, use upserts or idempotent insert patterns and include a short TTL index for ephemeral test documents so repeated runs do not accumulate test artifacts.
Avoid sending raw PII or sensitive balance-level data to external LLMs; send only aggregated, de-identified metrics and ensure the LLM path is disabled or mocked when OPENAI_API_KEY is missing.
Use explain() and server-side profiling to check aggregation plans and index usage and adjust indexes or pipeline ordering if the explain shows collection scans or excessive memory usage.
Monitor cluster-level metrics (CPU, I/O, RU/s or equivalent), set alerts for throttle/slow queries, and instrument the app to capture query latency and aggregation cost to detect regressions early.
Prefer per-collection or per-database least-privilege credentials rather than a single account key with full access; rotate credentials regularly and revoke keys used in test runs.

When presenting computed Basel III ratios, compute numerators and denominators atomically in a single aggregation pipeline stage where possible to avoid inconsistent snapshots across multiple queries.
